A discussion examines potential pathways to end the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, highlighting comments from Marco Rubio regarding a proposed US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral meeting. Rubio pointed out that the core of the conflict centres on the Donbas region and noted, "This war is only going to end diplomatically." The discussion also reviews global peace initiatives, including diplomatic efforts by India, proposals involving Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and an Egyptian plan. It underscores the extensive global ramifications of prolonged hostilities, spanning disrupted energy and wheat supplies, refugee migration, and post-war reconstruction costs estimated in multiple trillions of dollars.
'Unlikely That You Would See Any Trade Agreement Before Midterms': Alexander Slater
Speaking on the ongoing negotiations between New Delhi and Washington, former Managing Director of the US-India Business Council Alexander Slater analysed the key obstacles delaying a bilateral trade agreement. Slater noted that while both governments announced a framework agreement earlier in the year, substantive progress remains slow, remarking, 'I think it would be very unlikely that you would see any trade agreement announced between the two sides before the midterm elections.' He highlighted that past negotiations have consistently faced hurdles over issues such as totalization of benefits and agricultural tariffs. Slater also pointed to shifts in the geopolitical environment, including India's purchases of Russian oil and tariff waivers under the Graham Act. Furthermore, he emphasized the critical role of people-to-people ties, warning that recent visa disruptions could threaten bilateral technology cooperation and choke off a valuable source of human capital for the United States.

articles.title: Domestic companies need strategic approach to tap India-Europe FTA gains: FICCI - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Domestic companies need strategic approach to tap India-Europe FTA gains: FICCI  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
FICCI says MSMEs must upgrade product quality, meet European sustainability standards and integrate into regional supply chains to convert the India-EU free trade agreement into sustained export growth.
FICCI Secretary General Anant Swarup said the real challenge would be to convert improved market access into sustained market penetration.
He said that although the agreement, concluded in January, presents an unprecedented opportunity for Indian MSMEs to expand their presence in the European market, tariff concessions alone will not translate into higher exports.
Swarup is accompanying Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who is on a two-day visit here to boost trade and investment ties between India and Germany, its largest EU trading partner.
He said that MSMEs can also benefit by becoming suppliers to larger Indian and European companies, particularly in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering components, chemicals and processed foods.
He noted that compliance with European standards will remain one of the most critical determinants of export success.
EU requirements relating to product safety, technical standards, sustainability, traceability and carbon emissions can be particularly challenging for smaller enterprises, he said, adding the EU's evolving regulatory framework, including CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) and other sustainability-related requirements, will require Indian businesses to invest in cleaner technologies, certification and compliance systems.
Three areas of support will be particularly important: information and market intelligence, testing and certification infrastructure, and technology and financial support, he said.
He elaborated that industry needs practical, product-specific guidance on tariff concessions, rules of origin, regulatory requirements and export opportunities.
Dedicated FTA helpdesks, sector-specific advisory services and buyer-seller platforms can bridge this information gap.
"India must expand internationally accredited testing laboratories and certification facilities, particularly in major export clusters. Greater cooperation between Indian and European conformity assessment bodies can help reduce duplication, costs and delays," the Secretary General said.
MSMEs will need access to affordable finance, modern technology, digital traceability systems and support for meeting environmental and sustainability standards.
He added that shared facilities and targeted technology-upgradation programmes can make these investments more affordable.
"The FTA provides an institutional framework for regulatory dialogue and cooperation. This should be actively leveraged to address technical barriers, improve transparency and facilitate greater recognition of testing and certification systems wherever feasible," Swarup said.
He also said that Indian firms should look at the FTA beyond immediate tariff benefits as it can catalyse European investment into India, encourage technology partnerships, strengthen integration into global value chains and support diversification of our export markets.
"The real opportunity is not simply to export more to Europe, but to position India as a trusted manufacturing and services partner in European supply chains. This can deliver sustained gains in investment, production, employment and technological capabilities," he added.
India and the EU announced the conclusion of negotiations for the free trade agreement on January 27.
It is expected to be signed in December this year and may come into force next year.
India's exports to EU countries dipped by 4.57 per cent to $72.4 billion in 2025-26 from $75.85 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 17 per cent of India's total merchandise shipments in the last fiscal.
Imports, on the other hand, rose by 9 per cent to $66.18 billion in 2025-26 from $60.68 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 9 per cent of India's total merchandise imports in the last fiscal.
The trade gap was in the favour of India. Some of the European nations are major investors in India, and they include the Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Sweden and Denmark.

articles.title: India will cut tariffs on New Zealand wine from 150% to as low as 25% - Vinetur
articles.summary: India will cut tariffs on New Zealand wine from 150% to as low as 25%  Vinetur
articles.full_text:
The free trade agreement phases in the reductions over 10 years, improving access to one of the world’s most protected wine markets
Wednesday, October 21, 2026
India is set to lower import duties on New Zealand wine under a free trade agreement between the two countries, opening the way for cheaper access to a market that has long had some of the highest wine tariffs in the world.
According to Rural News Group, the agreement entered into force earlier this month. The report said Indian tariffs on wine begin at 150% and will be reduced over 10 years. For eligible New Zealand wine, the duty is scheduled to fall from 150% to either 25% or 50%, depending on the wine’s value. The agreement also includes a provision that would give New Zealand any better tariff treatment India later grants to another trade partner for the same products.
That clause could matter well beyond New Zealand’s wine industry. In the beverage sector, lower duties can improve access to a large consumer market, and the guarantee of future tariff improvements could change how exporters from different countries compete for shelf space and restaurant sales in India. If India offers deeper cuts to other wine-producing nations in future trade deals, New Zealand producers would not be left at a tariff disadvantage on covered products.
New Zealand Winegrowers says the Indian market has been growing from a low base. Alistair Buchanan, the group’s general manager for export and engagement, said India imported NZ$10 million of New Zealand wine and spirits in 2022 and about NZ$12 million in the past fiscal year. The figures cover both wine and spirits, but they point to a market that industry officials see as having room to expand as trade barriers come down.
Buchanan said the tariff cuts would improve the competitiveness of New Zealand wine in India. He also said the agreement would help New Zealand compete on a more level playing field in a country that already has a domestic wine industry. New Zealand Winegrowers notes that India is the fifth largest grower and producer of wine in Asia, which means imported bottles compete not only with other foreign suppliers but also with local producers.
For New Zealand exporters, the size of the tariff change is important because a 150% duty can sharply raise final retail prices and limit the number of consumers willing to buy imported wine. A step-down to 25% or 50% over time would not remove all barriers, but it would significantly narrow the price gap that tariffs create. That could help importers, distributors, restaurants, and retailers test a wider range of products in the market.
The agreement fits into New Zealand’s broader push to expand exports in faster-growing economies. Rural News Group reported that India also agreed to eliminate tariffs on kiwifruit, while tariffs on other key products will be reduced gradually. For Wellington, the deal is part of a larger trade strategy aimed at gaining better access for agricultural exports in countries where demand is rising.
The report, however, included different descriptions of the agreement’s status. It said the pact had entered into force earlier this month, but it also quoted Buchanan as saying the trade agreement was under consideration by New Zealand’s parliament and was expected to be ratified in the near future. That suggests some domestic steps or implementation details may still have been in process at the time of publication.
Even with that uncertainty over timing, the direction of the policy is clear. India’s market is becoming more important to wine exporters because of its size, urban growth, and the gradual development of a premium drinks segment. Lower import duties do not guarantee rapid sales growth, but they can make foreign wine more competitive and encourage importers to build distribution over time.
For producers in other wine-exporting countries, the New Zealand deal is also a signal to watch. Preferential tariff access can shift competitive balance in markets where duties remain high, especially when price-sensitive buyers compare imported brands. If the agreed reductions are carried out as described, New Zealand suppliers would gain a clearer route into India, while rival exporters may face pressure to seek similar terms through their own trade negotiations.

The dialogue explores the rationale behind Washington's waiver on Russian fuel imports, where global economic stabilization and preventing worldwide fuel price inflation emerged as immediate imperatives. articles.title: Rubio meets Jaishankar in Mumbai, says India-US trade deal is ‘very, very close’ - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Rubio meets Jaishankar in Mumbai, says India-US trade deal is ‘very, very close’  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The US secretary of state said a small number of issues remain to be resolved, expressing hope that the agreement would be finalised shortly.
Rubio said the two sides were close to finalising the pact, with only a few issues remaining. He expressed hope that the outstanding matters would be resolved shortly.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement. I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio said, as per AP.
Energy cooperation in focus
Rubio urged India to expand energy trade with the US, saying greater purchases could help diversify India's energy supplies and meet its large domestic demand.
Washington also discussed Venezuela and other potential sources of energy for India.
The US State Department said Rubio and Jaishankar discussed energy security and defence cooperation, while reaffirming the importance of advancing the bilateral strategic partnership.
The secretary of state also encouraged greater Indian purchases of US technologies and systems, saying these could strengthen the security and prosperity of both countries.
Trade deal nearing conclusion
The latest remarks signal progress in negotiations on the India-US trade agreement, which have faced difficulties amid differences over tariffs and India's purchases of Russian crude oil.
The two countries have been working towards an agreement after trade negotiations stalled. The remaining issues are yet to be resolved, and Rubio's comments indicate that a final agreement has not yet been concluded.
Jaishankar said after the meeting that the two sides had exchanged views on advancing bilateral ties, with a focus on trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people links.
"Our ties have indeed come a long way. History records that many Americans were supportive of India's struggle for independence. After that, whether it was infrastructure and education or food, agriculture, and technology, our partnership has made a real difference to India's development. Conversely, Indian talent and Indian skills have helped shape the tech era in the United States," said Jaishankar added.
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and other officials were also present at the meeting.
Rubio to visit Reliance refinery
Rubio's India visit also includes a trip to Jamnagar in Gujarat, where he is expected to meet Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani and visit the company's refinery complex.
The visit is aimed in part at discussing expanded energy cooperation, including opportunities to increase India's purchases of energy supplies from the US and other sources.
Rubio also paid tribute to victims of the November 2008 Mumbai terror attacks at the memorial at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel during his Mumbai engagements.

Marco Rubio defended US immigration curbs, urged India to diversify crude imports, backed deeper nuclear and defence cooperation, ruled out Pakistan ties coming at India's expense and called for a diplomatic end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday said India and the United States are close to reaching a trade agreement, with only a few issues remaining under negotiation, expressing optimism that the deal would provide greater certainty for businesses in both countries.
In an exclusive interview with India Today TV, Rubio said he could not foresee anything preventing an agreement, although he declined to disclose the remaining points of contention or whether Washington would offer India the competitive tariff advantage it was seeking in an interim trade deal.
"We are very close," Rubio said, adding that only a few items remained under discussion. He said the agreement must benefit both countries and provide businesses with clarity on the rules governing bilateral trade and investment.
"The point of having an agreement is to be able to have certainty so that people know they can invest, people know what the rules are that are going to govern trade and commerce between the two countries," he said.
The top Trump official was responding to concerns about continuity in trade policy and the possibility of repeated tariff revisions, including in the context of the Super 301 provision of retaliatory tariffs. He did not spell out how the proposed agreement would address these concerns but said predictability was one of the principal objectives of the negotiations.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who joined Rubio for the interview, described the bilateral relationship as stronger than ever across several sectors, including trade, information technology, pharmaceuticals and defence.
Gor said bilateral trade had increased from around USD 20 billion 15 years ago to usd 240 billion, arguing that investments by Indian and American companies were creating jobs in both countries.
He cited investments by Indian companies in the US, including multi-billion-dollar facilities being developed by the Essar group, as examples of the economic benefits flowing in both directions. Gor also said American technology companies operating in India complemented employment in the US rather than simply shifting jobs overseas.
H-1B VISA RESTRICTIONS NOT AIMED AT INDIA, SAYS RUBIO
Addressing concerns over higher visa costs and restrictions affecting Indian professionals and students, Rubio defended the Trump administration's immigration policies, saying they were part of a broader reform and were not specifically directed at India.
He acknowledged that the changes affected Indians seeking to work in the US and American businesses seeking to hire them, but said the policies applied to countries across the world.
"The United States has had a broken immigration system," Rubio said, citing unlawful immigration, alleged fraud and abuse in business-related immigration programmes and concerns among American workers about competition for jobs.
He said the administration wanted an immigration system that worked for the US economy and its citizens.
The Secretary argued that concerns over foreign workers taking up highly skilled jobs needed to be addressed as the administration pursued its goal of rebuilding American industry. He maintained that the policy changes were not India-specific, even if their impact was more pronounced in countries whose professionals make extensive use of US work visa programmes.
Gor echoed Rubio's position, saying the changes were not targeted at any individual country and arguing that Washington needed to reset its immigration policies.
He said the principle of "America First" did not mean the US wanted to act alone, adding that Washington expected other countries to understand its decision to prioritise its own national interests.
US WANTS INDIA TO BUY MORE AMERICAN CRUDE
On energy cooperation, Rubio said Washington wanted New Delhi to diversify its sources of energy by purchasing more crude oil from the US and other countries in the West, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing imports from Russia.
Asked about President Donald Trump's decision to allow additional energy flows into the global market, including a temporary waiver of sanctions affecting Russian oil purchases, Rubio said the administration was considering the wider effects of the Russia-Ukraine war and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
He said the temporary measure was intended to increase supplies in the global market at a time when diesel prices were high across the world.
Rubio stressed US foreign policy had to account for the wider global economic consequences of conflicts rather than be viewed through the lens of a single country or crisis.
Rubio argued that India had already been diversifying its energy sources and that greater reliance on a wider range of suppliers would serve its interests.
"It's not so much about buying less Russian oil than it is about buying more US crude or Venezuelan or others from the Western Hemisphere," he said.
He also highlighted India's refining capacity, saying the country could process more crude oil and attract investments to expand its refining infrastructure.
Rubio's visit to a refinery operated by Reliance Industries in Jamnagar in Gujarat, was an opportunity to understand its operations and its potential role in processing more crude from the Western Hemisphere, he said. He also pointed to the company's investment in a facility in Brownsville, Texas, which he said was expected to come online by 2029.
INDIA COULD BE AMONG FIRST COUNTRIES TO GET US SMALL MODULAR REACTORS
The US State Secretary also indicated that India could become one of the first international markets for American small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs), following India's decision to open parts of its civil nuclear sector to private participation.
He credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government with passing the SHANTI Bill, which he said enabled private technology and new equipment to enter India's nuclear sector.
Rubio acknowledged that regulatory challenges remained and that the process would take time, given the complexity of nuclear technology and the long-term nature of the partnership.
"India is one of the first places that the United States is looking at possibly to have our first SMRs internationally," he said.
He added that discussions had taken place in Washington, New Delhi and Mumbai, where India's nuclear regulatory agency is based and expressed confidence that cooperation would progress.
According to Rubio, the regulatory process was still under way, cautioning that the partnership would take time to develop because of the complexity of the technology and the long-term implications of nuclear cooperation.
'US-PAKISTAN TIES WILL NOT COME AT INDIA'S EXPENSE'

Asked how the US would ensure that closer ties with Pakistan did not come at the expense of India's fight against terrorism, Rubio said Washington had longstanding relations with both countries and hoped to use its engagement with Pakistan to influence its decisions.
"In no way does the relationship with Pakistan come at the expense of our relationship with India," he said.
Rubio said the US shared India's concerns about terrorism and cited American operations against Islamic State and al-Qaeda, as well as the killing of al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, as examples of Washington's counterterrorism efforts.
He also referred to US counterterrorism operations in parts of Africa, arguing that Washington had demonstrated a sustained commitment to combating extremist groups and ideologies that threaten both countries.
Asked about his diplomatic engagement during Operation Sindoor following the Pahalgam terror attack, Rubio declined to disclose details of his conversations with the Indian and Pakistani leadership.
He said the US was willing to play a constructive role whenever tensions between countries risked escalating into a wider conflict.
The objective, he said, was to prevent war and encourage countries to pursue cooperation in business and commerce.
Rubio added that any diplomatic solution would require both sides to engage and make concessions, while acknowledging that getting the parties to the negotiating table would not, by itself, resolve their differences.
DEFENCE COOPERATION AND QUAD GAIN MOMENTUM
Ambassoder Gor said defence cooperation between India and the US was at an all-time high, pointing to joint military exercises, co-production and the presence of American defence companies in India.
He cited the participation of around 500 US Army personnel in the Yudh Abhyas exercise and the involvement of American F-35 fighter jets in the Tarang Shakti exercise as examples of expanding military engagement.
The envoy added that Tarang Shakti marked the first time F-35 fighter jets had participated in a joint exercise in India and the aircraft were deployed only to countries Washington trusted, presenting their participation as an indication of the depth of the defence partnership.

Berlin [Germany], October 22 (ANI): Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday expressed confidence that the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) would move rapidly towards signing and could become operational within the next four to five months, urging Indian and German businesses to begin preparations to maximise its benefits.
Addressing an India-Germany business roundtable here, Goyal said companies should start identifying potential customers and collaborators, exchanging product samples and quality requirements, and discussing pricing rather than wait for the agreement to come into force.
"This is the time we need to see businesses start probably doing sampling, exchanging notes of quality required, exchanging pricing, get everything in order so that when the trade agreement comes into effect, we be the first off the block, get the maximum advantage of this agreement," he said.

India-EU FTA may be operational in January-March, says Piyush Goyal
Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the India-EU trade pact would be signed by the end of 2026, while warning that European regulations and tariffs could hurt trade
Listen to This Article
India's free trade agreement (FTA) with the European Union (EU) may come into effect in the first quarter of 2027 after being signed by the end of 2026, Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday.
"The EU agreement was announced on the 27th of January and will be signed before the end of the calendar year 2026," Goyal said at the Berlin Global Dialogue in Germany. "And will be operationalised probably in the first quarter of 2027," he added.
Goyal is currently on a six-day visit to Germany and the Netherlands, which will conclude on Tuesday, ahead of the signing of the India-EU trade agreement. The visit is aimed at deepening strategic economic partnerships, expanding bilateral trade and advancing industrial and technological collaboration.
The Indian minister also cautioned that the various regulations and standards rolled out by the EU not only pose non-tariff barriers to trade but may also hurt the European economy.
"What is Europe doing? They are shooting themselves in their own feet. More and more regulations, more and more restrictions on themselves. Closing their borders--something which actually helped them become a developed set of nations," Goyal said.
Also Read
"You put a CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) on yourself, you put a 50 per cent import duty to bring steel into your country-- you are inviting disaster," Goyal added.
The EU’s safeguard regime for steel, which came into effect on July 1, provides tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for shipments. Steel imports within the TRQ attract zero duty in the EU, while imports above the quota are subject to a 50 per cent tariff. The EU’s total annual duty-free steel quota limit stands at 18.3 million tonnes (mt).
New Delhi has secured a steel quota of over 1.9 mt under the EU's country-specific and residual quotas. Indian government officials estimate that the country's annual steel exports to the EU may stand at 2.8 mt.
India exported 3.8 mt of steel worth $3.4 billion to the EU in 2025-26, according to data available with the Department of Commerce.
"Bear in mind, the world is a reciprocal world now," Goyal said at the event. "In this reciprocal world, you bring in a regulation and stop some other country from working with you. They will bring in two regulations which will hurt your businesses," he added.
The EU's CBAM has also been a concern for India. In fact, it was the longest-standing sticking point during New Delhi's negotiations with Brussels for the FTA.
Under the trade deal, India and the EU have also agreed to work together to build capacity in India for CBAM verification, including recognition of Indian verification agencies.
India wants to ensure that exporters have sufficient domestic verification capacity to provide the emissions documentation required under CBAM rather than depend on a limited pool of overseas agencies. Additionally, India is working on its Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and discussing carbon pricing with the EU.

articles.title: Manufacturing Shift from China to India: Key Reasons - Business Outreach Magazine
articles.summary: Manufacturing Shift from China to India: Key Reasons  Business Outreach Magazine
articles.full_text:
For three decades, “made in China” was simply how the world’s electronics, cars and clothes got made. That machine hasn’t broken down. But a growing number of multinational companies no longer want to depend on it alone.
The manufacturing shift from China to India has picked up real pace over the last two years. Tariff shocks, pandemic-era shutdowns and unease about relying on one country for critical production pushed boardrooms to ask a hard question: what if China becomes harder to work with tomorrow? India, with its scale, its incentives and a fast-growing consumer base, has become one of the loudest answers.
This piece looks at why the manufacturing shift from China to India is happening now, and where India still has work to do before it can call itself a genuine alternative.
Quick Glance
| Factor | Why It Matters | 
| China Plus One Strategy | Spreads production across more than one country | 
| PLI scheme and Make in India | Rewards investment tied to real output | 
| Electronics Manufacturing in India | Fastest-growing proof point of the shift | 
| Global Supply Chain Diversification | Cuts exposure to any single country’s problems | 
| Foreign Direct Investment in India | Signals long-term confidence, not just a trend | 
China Plus One Isn’t a Buzzword Anymore
The China Plus One Strategy sounds like consultant-speak, but the logic is simple: keep China operations running, and build a second production base elsewhere so one bad year doesn’t sink the whole supply chain.
Container ships stuck outside ports, factories shut for weeks during COVID-19, components that couldn’t be sourced for months, tariff back-and-forth between the US and China all of it made the case too strong to ignore. Here’s what’s actually pushing the shift:
- Cutting reliance on a single country for critical production
- Managing tariff and geopolitical risk
- Building a backup line that can absorb shocks
- Getting closer to new, fast-growing consumer markets
India isn’t the only beneficiary; Vietnam, Mexico and Indonesia compete for the same investment. But India’s scale gives it an edge smaller economies can’t match, which is why the China Plus One Strategy so often ends with a factory in Gujarat, Tamil Nadu or Uttar Pradesh. It rarely means leaving China entirely; companies are simply refusing to put every egg in one basket.
Government Policy Is Doing the Heavy Lifting
India Manufacturing Growth over the last five years hasn’t happened by accident; deliberate policy has shaped it as much as market forces have.
The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme sits at the centre, with a total outlay of roughly ₹1.91 lakh crore across 14 sectors, tying cash incentives directly to what a company produces and exports. According to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, as of March 31, 2026, the scheme had drawn actual investments of more than ₹2.40 lakh crore, generated over 14.15 lakh direct and indirect jobs, and pushed exports past ₹15.2 lakh crore since inception. That’s the kind of number that makes Foreign Direct Investment in India look like a working strategy rather than a policy slogan, spanning mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and telecom equipment.
The government’s Make in India push has run alongside the PLI scheme since 2014, nudging sectors toward higher local value addition. Neither works alone a company still weighs the incentive against land costs, power, logistics and clearance timelines.
Electronics Manufacturing in India Is Where the Shift Shows Up Most
If one industry proves the manufacturing shift from China to India is real, it’s electronics.
Apple began assembling iPhones in India in 2017, before the PLI scheme even existed, but the scheme accelerated everything after. Apple now runs five iPhone assembly plants in India three under Tata Group entities, two under Foxconn – backed by a supplier network of close to 45 companies, according to Angel One’s February 2026 reporting. India assembled iPhones worth roughly $22 billion in the year to March 2025, up nearly 60% year-on-year, with $17.4 billion exported, per IBEF. By calendar 2025, iPhone exports had climbed to $23 billion, making the iPhone India’s single most valuable export product that year, per Business Today’s April 2026 coverage.
Tariffs pushed this along. Techwire Asia reported in March 2026 that China-assembled iPhones faced US import duties near 55%, against roughly 10% for India-made devices a gap wide enough that Apple reportedly chartered cargo flights in March 2025 to move close to $2 billion worth of India-made iPhones to the US ahead of fresh tariffs.
Competition inside Apple’s own supply chain shows how fast Electronics Manufacturing in India has matured. Tata Electronics, a late entrant that only started assembling iPhones after acquiring Wistron’s India unit in November 2023, has nearly caught up to Foxconn on exports over the five-year PLI period through FY26:
| Metric (FY22–FY26, PLI period) | Figure | 
| Tata Electronics: exported iPhone value | $26.3 billion | 
| Foxconn: exported iPhone value | $25.6 billion | 
| Foxconn: domestic-market iPhone value | $12.4 billion | 
| Tata Electronics: domestic-market iPhone value | $6.3 billion | 
| Apple India vendor component exports to China (FY26) | ~$2.5 billion, rising toward $3.5 billion | 
Source: Business Standard, July 2026; The Week, May 2026. A reversal is underway on that last line India’s component makers are now shipping parts to China rather than the other way round, something that would have sounded far-fetched only a few years ago. China still assembles most of the world’s iPhones, but the direction here is unmistakable.
Diversification, Workforce and Home Demand
Global Supply Chain Diversification answers what the pandemic exposed a single-location supply chain breaks the moment one link fails. A company running plants in both China and India can shift output if a strike, lockdown or tariff hits one location.
India’s other advantages reinforce that logic:
- A large, young workforce and a growing pool of engineers though productivity and technical skill matter more than headcount
- A domestic market for smartphones, cars and appliances large enough to justify local production on its own
- Local manufacturing that feeds Foreign Direct Investment in India by letting companies serve consumers at home while building export capacity in parallel
Automotive and Semiconductors: The Next Frontier
India’s established automotive sector gives it a real shot at fresh investment in EV components, batteries and power electronics.
Semiconductors are the longer game. India is building that ecosystem largely from scratch Tata Electronics alone has committed roughly ₹1.26 trillion toward semiconductor fabrication and ATMP facilities, per Business Standard’s July 2026 reporting. Nobody expects India to rival Taiwan soon, but the investment suggests India Manufacturing Growth is climbing the value chain, not just assembling.
What India Still Has to Fix
The opportunity is real, but so are the gaps:
- Infrastructure – power, roads, ports has improved unevenly across states
- The supplier ecosystem is still thin next to China’s dense clusters of component makers
- Several industries still import raw materials they could eventually make at home
- Vocational training hasn’t kept pace with the ambition behind Make in India
- Regulatory friction – land acquisition, environmental clearances, state-level tax rules still slows decisions on billion-dollar factories, where predictability often matters more than the incentive itself
Is India Actually Replacing China?
Not really, and framing it that way misses the point. China still has a mature supplier network, decades of know-how, and industrial clusters that took generations to build none of that disappears because a few factories move to Gujarat. What’s changing is India’s share of the pie, not China’s position at the top. Some multinationals will keep manufacturing in China while adding India capacity; others will make India their base for specific products, the way Apple has with iPhones bound for the US. The likely outcome, years out, is multiple manufacturing hubs rather than one country doing everything.
Key Takeaways
- The manufacturing shift from China to India runs on the China Plus One Strategy, not a wholesale exit from China.
- The PLI scheme and Make in India have turned Foreign Direct Investment in India into measurable output.
- Electronics Manufacturing in India, led by Apple’s supply chain, is the clearest proof point.
- Global Supply Chain Diversification is a multi-year process, not an overnight switch.
- India still has real gaps in infrastructure, supplier depth, skills and regulation.
Conclusion
The manufacturing shift from China to India isn’t one event it’s the sum of smaller decisions: a tariff calculation here, a PLI application there, a supplier relationship built over two years. Supply chain diversification, government incentives, a large workforce and a genuinely large domestic market have pushed in the same direction at roughly the same time, and that convergence is what makes the shift feel real.
Apple’s expanding iPhone production is the clearest evidence, but automotive components, pharmaceuticals and semiconductors are moving along a similar path, just earlier on. If India keeps attracting investment while closing its supplier, skills and infrastructure gaps, India Manufacturing Growth could become one of the more consequential economic stories of this decade not because India replaced China, but because the world stopped betting everything on one country.

Indian firms must build EU buyer links to gain from FTA, says Ficci
Ficci Secretary General said firms must identify products with significant tariff advantages, strengthen ties with European buyers and upgrade quality to convert market access into sustained exports
Listen to This Article
Indian companies need to adopt a more strategic approach to the European market to fully benefit from the free trade agreement, as tariff concessions alone will not lead to higher exports, industry chamber FICCI said on Thursday.
FICCI Secretary General Anant Swarup said the real challenge would be to convert improved market access into sustained market penetration.
He said that although the agreement, concluded in January, presents an unprecedented opportunity for Indian MSMEs to expand their presence in the European market, tariff concessions alone will not translate into higher exports.
"Indian companies will need to adopt a more strategic approach to the European market. This includes identifying products where tariff advantages are significant, building relationships with European buyers, upgrading product quality, and integrating into European supply chains," he told PTI.
Swarup is accompanying Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who is on a two-day visit here to boost trade and investment ties between India and Germany, its largest EU trading partner.
Also Read
He said that MSMEs can also benefit by becoming suppliers to larger Indian and European companies, particularly in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering components, chemicals and processed foods.
He noted that compliance with European standards will remain one of the most critical determinants of export success.
EU requirements relating to product safety, technical standards, sustainability, traceability and carbon emissions can be particularly challenging for smaller enterprises, he said, adding the EU's evolving regulatory framework, including CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) and other sustainability-related requirements, will require Indian businesses to invest in cleaner technologies, certification and compliance systems.
Three areas of support will be particularly important: information and market intelligence, testing and certification infrastructure, and technology and financial support, he said.
He elaborated that industry needs practical, product-specific guidance on tariff concessions, rules of origin, regulatory requirements and export opportunities.
Dedicated FTA helpdesks, sector-specific advisory services and buyer-seller platforms can bridge this information gap.
"India must expand internationally accredited testing laboratories and certification facilities, particularly in major export clusters. Greater cooperation between Indian and European conformity assessment bodies can help reduce duplication, costs and delays," the Secretary General said.
MSMEs will need access to affordable finance, modern technology, digital traceability systems and support for meeting environmental and sustainability standards.
He added that shared facilities and targeted technology-upgradation programmes can make these investments more affordable.
"The FTA provides an institutional framework for regulatory dialogue and cooperation. This should be actively leveraged to address technical barriers, improve transparency and facilitate greater recognition of testing and certification systems wherever feasible," Swarup said.
He also said that Indian firms should look at the FTA beyond immediate tariff benefits as it can catalyse European investment into India, encourage technology partnerships, strengthen integration into global value chains and support diversification of our export markets.
"The real opportunity is not simply to export more to Europe, but to position India as a trusted manufacturing and services partner in European supply chains. This can deliver sustained gains in investment, production, employment and technological capabilities," he added.
India and the EU announced the conclusion of negotiations for the free trade agreement on January 27.
It is expected to be signed in December this year and may come into force next year.

articles.title: Is It a South Asian Spring? Bangladesh, Nepal and the Rising Tide of Protest in India - Countercurrents
articles.summary: Is It a South Asian Spring? Bangladesh, Nepal and the Rising Tide of Protest in India  Countercurrents
articles.full_text:
An assessment of youth mobilisation, democratic discontent, economic insecurity and the future of political accountability in South Asia
Is This a Region in Political Turmoil
South Asia is witnessing a powerful wave of political mobilisation that raises an important question: Is the region approaching a “South Asian Spring”? The dramatic political upheaval in Bangladesh in 2024, the youth-led protests in Nepal in 2025, and continuing demonstrations over governance, corruption, unemployment, civil liberties and political accountability in India suggest that democratic discontent is becoming increasingly visible across national borders. The term “South Asian Spring” evokes the Arab Spring of 2010-2012, when mass demonstrations challenged authoritarian governments across West Asia and North Africa. However, South Asia’s political circumstances are different. Bangladesh experienced the collapse of Sheikh Hasina’s government in August 2024; Nepal underwent a major political crisis in September 2025, following youth protests against a social media ban and broader grievances over corruption and governance. India, meanwhile, has a much larger and more institutionally complex democracy, where protests occur through diverse political, social, student, labour and civil-society movements.
These developments should not be treated as evidence of a single, coordinated regional revolution. Rather, they reveal a shared crisis of political trust. Young citizens increasingly expect governments to deliver employment, transparency, social justice and meaningful participation. When established political institutions fail to meet these expectations, streets, universities and digital platforms become alternative arenas of democratic expression. The central question, therefore, is not simply whether a South Asian spring has begun, but whether the region’s political systems can respond to popular demands without repression, instability or democratic backsliding.
Bangladesh: From Student Protest to Regime Change
Bangladesh provides the most striking example of mass mobilisation transforming national politics. In July 2024, student protests initially focused on the public-sector job quota system. The movement expanded rapidly after violent confrontations, casualties and growing public anger over the government’s response. Its demands broadened from employment reform to accountability, democratic rights and the resignation of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. On 5 August 2024, Hasina left office and departed Bangladesh after weeks of escalating demonstrations. The Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus subsequently established an interim administration. The scale of the crisis was devastating. The United Nations human rights office estimated that as many as 1,400 people may have been killed between 1 July and 15 August 2024, with thousands more injured. This was an estimate, not a final judicially established death toll, but it illustrates the extraordinary human cost of the confrontation.
The uprising exposed several structural weaknesses. First, young graduates faced intense competition for secure employment. Second, the quota system became a symbol of perceived political favouritism and unequal access to opportunity. Third, restrictions on dissent and the violent suppression of demonstrations undermined the government’s legitimacy. Finally, economic grievances converged with broader concerns about political accountability and democratic participation. Bangladesh demonstrates how a movement that begins with a seemingly narrow policy demand can become a national challenge to political authority. Once citizens believe that formal channels cannot deliver justice, the legitimacy of the entire governing system may come under question. Yet regime change does not automatically guarantee democratic consolidation. The transition must be judged by whether it produces credible elections, protects minorities, establishes accountability for abuses and restores confidence in public institutions. The removal of a government is a political turning point, not proof that all the underlying problems have been solved.
Nepal: The Gen Z Revolt and the Crisis of Political Credibility
Nepal’s September 2025 protests added another dimension to the regional story. Youth-led demonstrations erupted after the government restricted access to major social media platforms. The ban became a focal point for wider frustration over corruption, nepotism, political privilege and the limited opportunities available to younger generations. The protests escalated into a major political crisis, with violence, casualties and the resignation of Prime Minister K. P. Sharma Oli. The episode revealed a strong link between digital freedoms and political accountability. The social media controversy alone cannot explain Nepal’s political instability. Since becoming a republic in 2008, the country has experienced frequent changes of government and persistent disputes over the performance of political elites. For many young Nepalis, repeated leadership changes have not translated into sufficiently visible improvements in employment, public services or economic opportunity.
The economic context is particularly important. World Bank and other international assessments have repeatedly highlighted Nepal’s dependence on remittances, its limited capacity to create productive domestic employment and the scale of labour migration. Remittances have represented roughly a quarter of Nepal’s GDP recently, making overseas employment central to household livelihoods and the wider economy. This dependence creates a political paradox: young citizens may possess greater educational qualifications and digital awareness than previous generations, yet many see migration as their most realistic route to economic security. Nepal’s experience, therefore, highlights three important features of contemporary protest: the mobilisation of digitally connected youth, the erosion of confidence in established political parties, and the growing perception that public institutions serve political networks more effectively than they do ordinary citizens. As in Bangladesh, however, the long-term outcome depends on what follows the demonstrations. Institutional reform, credible political participation, and policies that create opportunities at home must accompany a change in leadership.
India: From Electoral Discontent to Youth-Led Political Mobilisation
India presents a more complex case. Unlike Bangladesh in August 2024 and Nepal in September 2025, India’s political landscape has not experienced a sudden nationwide uprising that overthrew the government. Nevertheless, protests over examination irregularities, unemployment, electoral transparency, corruption, civil liberties and social justice reveal substantial areas of public dissatisfaction. In 2026, youth-led mobilisation around examination-system reform and political accountability brought these tensions into sharper focus. Reports on the emerging Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) movement describe demonstrations spreading across numerous states, with demands for accountability over examination controversies and broader governance concerns. A July 2026 report by India Today, citing protest-event data, recorded 412 events during a seven-day period, including 328 peaceful demonstrations, 63 involving intervention by police or other forces, and 21 that turned violent. The same report recorded 12,527 protest events in India between 1 January and 24 July 2026, the highest figure for that period since 2020. These figures describe recorded events, not the number of individual protesters, and should be interpreted accordingly.
The political significance of these protests lies in the distance between India’s economic ambitions and the everyday expectations of its young population. India has a substantial demographic dividend, but the benefits of a large working-age population depend on access to quality education, productive employment and fair recruitment. Allegations of paper leaks, irregularities, or administrative failures in competitive examinations have consequences that extend beyond individual candidates. Families invest years of time and savings in preparation, and repeated controversies can undermine confidence in public institutions. The problem is not simply unemployment; it is also the perceived unfairness of opportunity. Young people may accept difficult economic conditions more readily when recruitment is transparent and institutions are credible. They are less likely to accept them when they believe that political connections, privilege or administrative failures determine outcomes.
Electoral transparency has also emerged as a central issue. In October 2026, opposition parties and youth activists demonstrated in New Delhi over revisions to electoral rolls, seeking greater scrutiny of voter deletions and safeguards against wrongful disenfranchisement. The Election Commission’s processes and the government’s response to allegations require independent, evidence-based assessment. Claims that particular communities have been deliberately targeted should not be treated as facts without adequate verification. Nevertheless, questions concerning the accuracy of voter lists deserve transparent answers because electoral participation is fundamental to democratic legitimacy.
India’s institutional context remains distinct from that of its neighbours.
It has a constitutional framework, and India’s institutional context remains distinct from that of its neighbours, featuring regular elections, a competitive federal system, an active judiciary, and a long history of mass movements.
These elements create channels for expressing and addressing public grievances.
However, the existence of democratic institutions does not eliminate the obligation to protect peaceful assembly, freedom of expression, and equal political participation.

articles.title: 'As Close As You Can Be': Rubio & Trump Tease Landmark India-US Trade Pact - India Weekly
articles.summary: 'As Close As You Can Be': Rubio & Trump Tease Landmark India-US Trade Pact  India Weekly
articles.full_text:
- Rubio says India-US trade deal is “about as close as you can be”
- Trump says it will be “a much different kind of deal”
- Rubio urges India to buy more US energy and defense technology
- He calls India a “refining superpower” and pitches Venezuelan crude
INDIA and the United States are close to finalizing a trade deal, president Donald Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio said Tuesday, as Rubio urged New Delhi to step up purchases of American energy and defense systems.
“I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai, where he held talks with India's external affairs minister S Jaishankar.
“I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up. So I think that will happen shortly—we’re hoping, which it should—and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon. And perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter.”
In Washington, Trump said the two countries were “pretty close” to an agreement.
“They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal,” Trump said at the Oval Office. “It’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we’ve done.”
Energy and defense push
India’s Ministry of External Affairs said both sides welcomed progress in the negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding the agreement early.
The State Department said Rubio told Jaishankar that increased energy trade with the US could “play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains.”
Rubio also praised progress in defense and civil nuclear cooperation and “advocated for the increased purchase of US technologies and systems,” the department said.
Jaishankar said the two discussed trade, energy, technology, defense and people-to-people ties. US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who attended the meeting, described the talks as “productive.”
Before the meeting, Rubio laid a wreath at the Taj memorial in honor of the victims of the 2008 Mumbai attacks, which included six Americans.
Venezuela and Russian oil
Rubio described India as a “refining superpower” and pitched processing more Venezuelan crude in the country, noting that some Indian companies hold existing oil concessions in Venezuela.
Asked whether Washington was unhappy about India’s Russian oil purchases, he said India had made “substantial progress” in diversifying its energy sources.
“In the end, it’s not just about Russian oil; it’s about their desire to diversify, and obviously we think we can be a source of some of their energy inputs,” he said.
Rubio visits Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery on Wednesday.
Ties under strain
The visit, Rubio’s second to India in under five months, comes as relations remain strained over Washington’s unpredictable trade policies and tighter immigration rules.
India and the US announced a framework for the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement in February, but changes to US tariffs have forced further negotiations. India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal met US trade representative Jamieson Greer in Milwaukee and Washington earlier this month.

articles.title: Who was Sweety Akhtar, mother of 9-year-old executed by Saudi Arabia over adultery? - India Today
articles.summary: Who was Sweety Akhtar, mother of 9-year-old executed by Saudi Arabia over adultery?  India TodaySaudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts’ in a Mecca mosque  South China Morning PostNo, Photo Doesn’t Show Bangladeshi Nationals Who Were Executed in Saudi Arabia  The QuintBangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia  BBCSaudi Arabia Executes Two Bangladeshi Nationals  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Curr...
articles.full_text:
Married twice and abandoned by her second husband, Bangladeshi national Sweety Akhtar left her country to secure her daughter's future. But, she ended up in a Saudi Arabian prison and was executed over alleged adultery, leaving her family unaware of her death sentence until they learnt about it on Facebook.
Sweety Akhtar's last phone conversation with her father gave no hint that it would be their final one. Married while she was in Class 8, divorced, remarried and later abandoned by her second husband, Sweety Akhtar had left Bangladesh for Saudi Arabia to build a better future for her daughter. The youngest of five sisters, Sweety Akhtar came from a poor family in Tangail, where her father worked as a daily wage labourer. She left her daughter, now nine according to a relative, in her elder sister's care and moved to Saudi Arabia in March 2023 to work as a cleaner.
But within six months, she was in prison, and three years after her arrival in the Kingdom, she was executed for what Saudi authorities described as "immoral acts" inside a mosque in Mecca. She was executed alongside another Bangladeshi national, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir, who worked for the same company. According to a Bangladeshi consular memorandum, Sweety had been detained on allegations of adultery, while Nazrul was arrested under Saudi Arabia's cybercrime law.
On October 14, Saudi Arabia announced the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, Sweety Akhtar and Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir, following their conviction for acts described as immoral. The executions have sparked outrage in Bangladesh after its diplomatic mission said it had not been informed beforehand.
Sweety's family, meanwhile, learnt of her reported execution through others and Facebook, despite remaining in contact with her during her imprisonment. Her father said he last spoke to her on October 13, a day before the execution, but she never mentioned a death sentence. So, who was Sweety Akhtar?
MARRIED IN CLASS 8, ABANDONED BY SECOND HUSBAND
Sweety was born in Nagar Chhawali village in Mahera union of Mirzapur upazila, Tangail in central Bangladesh. Her parents, Md Fazal Mia and Johura Begum, had five daughters, of whom Sweety was the youngest.
According to Bangladeshi newspaper Prothom Alo, Sweety was married while studying in Class 8. The marriage broke down, and she returned to her parents' home with her daughter.
Under family pressure, she married again. Her father, who earned a daily wage, borrowed money to send Sweety's second husband to Saudi Arabia, but he stopped communicating with her after reaching the country.
Sweety's cousin Salma Akhtar told Prothom Alo that the repeated setbacks in her married life and the family's poverty prompted her to seek employment abroad.
Salma said Sweety's daughter, now nine years old, studies in Class 3 at a local primary school. Dhaka-based newspaper, The Daily Star, quoted Sweety's mother as saying the child was four years old.
FATHER BORROWED TAKA 1.5 LAKH TO SEND HER ABROAD
According to The Daily Star, Sweety's father, Fazal Mia, borrowed Taka 1.5 lakh to send her to Saudi Arabia. She travelled in March 2023 through a registered recruitment agency.
BBC Bangla reported that her passport had been issued in May 2022 and that Bangladesh's Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training cleared her for overseas employment in February 2023.
Sweety worked as a cleaner, reportedly inside Mecca's holy mosque complex. For the first five to six months, she sent money home.
Then the transactions stopped.
Her father told The Daily Star, "She sent money home for the first five months. One day, she called and told us she had been sent to jail."
ARRESTED IN AUGUST 2023, FAMILY TOLD A DIFFERENT STORY
A confidential October 18 consular memorandum obtained by The Daily Star showed that Sweety was detained on August 2, 2023, on allegations of adultery. Nazrul was detained a day earlier under Saudi Arabia's cybercrime law.
Both worked for Al Majal Company, according to the memorandum. Sweety was held at Jeddah Women's Prison.
But the explanation she gave her family was different. According to her father, Sweety claimed that some female colleagues had illegally purchased a car and that she had been arrested along with them, The Daily Star reported. Her relatives believe she was falsely implicated.
SWEETY AKHTAR CALLED HOME A DAY BEFORE EXECUTION
Even in prison, Sweety maintained contact with her family, sometimes calling every week and sometimes after a month.
BBC Bangla reported that her relatives knew she was imprisoned but did not know the precise charges. Sweety had discouraged further questions, promising to explain everything when she returned home.
Her father told Prothom Alo that they last spoke on October 13, after Maghrib (evening) prayers. She said nothing about her trial or sentence. The Daily Star separately quoted Fazal as saying that Sweety had suggested she might be released within two months.
Her elder sister told BBC Bangla that she discovered news of the death sentence through a Facebook video sent by a friend.
A FAMILY WAITING FOR ANSWERS
While speculations are being made over the execution of the two Bangladeshis, Dhaka is still awaiting the precise acts underlying the two convictions. The Bangladesh mission in Saudi Arabia said it received no advance notification. Dhaka has sought copies of the judgments and details of the proceedings. However, Riyadh has not responded to the queries.
Although Bangladesh's Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare disclosed the executed workers' identities on October 19, Sweety's family said it had still received no direct official confirmation. Her mother, Johura Begum, told Prothom Alo, "My daughter, you suffered so much, yet you didn't tell anyone. You didn't even tell me. Bring my daughter's body home. I want to see her."
For the family which borrowed money to send their daughter abroad, the hope of her returning with savings has now turned into a plea to bring her remains home.

Two people, including an Indian national, were killed and eight others injured on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) in a Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil hub, the kingdom’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed the Indian national’s death. “Saudi authorities have informed that one Indian national was among two people who unfortunately lost their lives in the attack on Dammam airport yesterday night and two Indian nationals were injured,” the Indian embassy wrote in a social media post on Thursday (October 22, 2026). “We are ascertaining further details and contacting the affected families. Our thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of the deceased and we wish speedy recovery of the injured.”
Airport operations and air traffic had returned to normal after brief disruptions, the Saudi aviation authority said.
Separately, the Houthis (Ansar Allah) claimed that Saudi Arabia had attacked a yacht carrying Indians in the Red Sea, adding that they were conducting rescue operations.
The Houthis, who control northern and northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sana’a, said they launched missile and drone attacks at the Saudi Ministry of Defence in Riyadh and the Dammam airport. They also struck a facility of Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned petroleum and natural gas company, in Yanbu, and the Abha International Airport in the southwest.
If Saudi Arabia continues to attack Yemen, “we will resort to major options we did not want to take, and we hold it responsible for the consequences,” the militants said, according to the Houthi-aligned Almasirah television.
The Iran-aligned rebels, who captured Sana’a in 2014 and expanded their territorial control along Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast last month, also claimed that the Saudi forces on Thursday targeted an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island in Red Sea, carrying 14 Indians.
“The [Houthi] Armed Forces are carrying out rescue operations for those on board, with further details to be provided later,” they said, according to Almasirah. “It indicated that this reckless behavior by the Saudi enemy threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, requiring the international community to stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions.”
The targeting of a civilian vessel carrying Indian nationals raises serious concerns about the safety of international navigation and the potential for civilian casualties, they added.
Saudi Arabia started bombing Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis captured Sana’a a few months earlier. In 2022, Riyadh and the Houthi leadership agreed to a ceasefire as part of a broader Iran-Saudi rapprochement. The ceasefire collapsed in July this year, in the midst of the U.S.-Iran war, as the Sana’a airport was bombed by Saudi Arabia to prevent an Iranian airline carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis then started attacking Saudi Arabia and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. They have also announced a blockade of Saudi ports in the Red Sea.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have stepped up attacks against Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, while the kingdom has intensified its air strikes on the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.
On Thursday (October 22, 2026), the Houthis said they will continue their operations against Saudi Arabia. “There will be siege for siege and escalation for escalation,” they said, adding that the strikes would continue until Saudi Arabia lifts its blockade of the Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

articles.title: India's core sector growth rate surges to 30-month high in September - IANS LIVE
articles.summary: India's core sector growth rate surges to 30-month high in September  IANS LIVE
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct 21 (IANS) The growth rate of India’s core sector industries surged to a 30-month high of 7.9 per cent in September, compared to the same month of the previous year, driven by the strong performance of the iron ore, electricity, coal refinery products, cement, and steel sectors, according to figures released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Wednesday.
The production of iron ore surged by as much as 18.4 per cent in September. Owing to intensive use of iron ore in the production process and its contribution to industrial development, it has been included in the list of core industries as a new item in the revised series of the index of core industries (ICI). Accordingly, the number of core industries has increased from eight to nine in the new series, which kicked in for the first time last month.
Electricity generation grew by 11.4 per cent during September while coal production went up by 10.7 per cent. The output of refinery products increased by 10.7 per cent during the month as demand for petroleum goods rose due to the higher level of economic activity.
The cement sector clocked a robust growth of 10.3 per cent while steel production was up 4.9 per cent during the month as demand stayed buoyant due to large government investments in big-ticket infrastructure projects such as highways, ports and railways.
However, fertilisers, natural gas, and crude oil witnessed negative growth in September.
The final index for the month of August 2026 has been revised from 119.2 to 120.4. Accordingly, the year-on-year growth rate has been revised from 4.8 per cent to 5.9 per cent.
Cumulative growth rate of the index of core industries during April-September 2026 now works out to 5.1 per cent compared to 2.5 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year, reflecting the acceleration in the growth of the infrastructure industries.
The Office of Economic Adviser, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has released the revised series of Index of Core Industries (ICI) with Base Year 2022-23 for the first time in July this year. The new series has replaced the earlier series of ICI with Base Year 2011- 12.

New Delhi [India], October 21 (ANI): Congress leader and former Chhattisgarh Deputy Chief Minister T S Singh Deo on Wednesday questioned the Centre over the India-US trade deal, alleging that details about the negotiations were being shared by visiting US officials rather than the Indian government.
He urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to inform Parliament about the terms of the agreement before signing it.
In a post on X, Singh Deo took a swipe at the government over the reported progress in trade negotiations and referred to remarks by a visiting American official at a press conference in Mumbai.
He also raised questions over India's crude oil purchases and defence procurement, suggesting that Washington was providing updates on matters concerning India's economic and strategic decisions.
He said, "Good news, India. Our trade deal is almost done. How do we know? Not from Parliament. Not from our own govt. We heard it from a visiting American Secretary of State at a press conference in Mumbai. He also had updates on which crude we are ready to refine, how pleased Washington is with where we buy our oil, and which American defence systems we should be buying next. Very thorough briefing. Our govt could take notes."
The Congress leader further questioned the transparency surrounding the negotiations, arguing that a trade agreement could have implications for farmers, small manufacturers and households.
Drawing a comparison with the Union Budget, Singh Deo criticised what he described as the lack of information being shared by the government with Parliament and the public.
"At this rate the next Budget may be announced at a US press briefing, with our Finance Minister invited as a special guest. A trade deal decides the price farmers get for their crops, the margin of a small manufacturer and the cost of fuel for every family. These are not details a nation should learn from a foreign minister's travel diary. Will the Prime Minister tell Parliament what India is giving and what it is getting before he signs?" he added.
Deo's remarks come after United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio revealed that the India-US trade deal is "incredibly close", indicating that finalisation is anticipated shortly.
Speaking to Network18, Rubio noted that while he is not directly engaged in the negotiations, which are handled through the trade representative, he has closely monitored the discussions and expects the agreement to materialise in a matter of weeks, not months.
"I'm not personally negotiating it; it's done through our trade representative, but I know, and I've been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months," said Rubio.
Elaborating on the meticulous final stages, he highlighted the necessity of absolute precision prior to public announcements to safeguard bilateral ties of such high importance.
Addressing queries concerning comparative rates for India alongside other nations, Rubio affirmed that the overarching outcome remains highly advantageous.
Commenting on the sheer magnitude and diversity of the nation, the US Secretary of State underscored the necessity of broad exploratory visits rather than confining diplomatic engagements strictly to capitals. (ANI)

Backed by billions of dollars in subsidies, India's high-tech manufacturing sector is steadily integrating into global supply chains, but still faces challenges related to added value and investment efficiency.
This experience highlights the requirements for Vietnam in implementing Resolution 57: attracting investment must go hand in hand with enhancing endogenous technological capacity and mastering high-value-added stages.
Optimists argue that Apple's move to shift some iPhone production to India helps the country reduce its dependence on China and improve its position in the global supply chain. Currently, about a quarter of iPhones are manufactured in factories near Chennai, providing jobs for tens of thousands of workers.
However, skeptics argue that much of the activity remains focused on final assembly, which creates little added value. Nevertheless, Indian factories have begun taking on more stages, from assembling components onto circuit boards to manufacturing motherboards.
The core question is whether these advances are commensurate with the state subsidies. If competitiveness cannot be maintained without budgetary support, the gains of India's manufacturing sector risk reversing.

Smartphones use many high-value components such as circuit boards, camera modules, and screens. To truly improve its position in the production chain, the export value of finished phones needs to increase faster than the import of input components.
However, the evaluation is not simple because many imported components are also used in electric vehicles , solar panels, and other equipment.
In 2023, former Reserve Bank of India Governor Raghuram Rajan and two colleagues developed three scenarios, assuming that 40%, 60%, or 80% of imported components in the multipurpose category were used in mobile phones. In all three cases, India's mobile phone trade balance remained in deficit. The research team argued that the increase in finished phone exports was not enough to demonstrate that the country's manufacturing capacity had reached a breakthrough.
Newer analysis shows that the trade balance remains in deficit, but the gap between component imports and phone exports has narrowed. This indicates progress in domestic manufacturing, although it is not yet possible to say that India has mastered the majority of the product's value.
Value added remains limited.

Indian suppliers have expanded into more complex processes, but the lack of mastery in the production of memory chips, processors, lenses, displays, and batteries still limits the ability to create domestic value.
With the iPhone 14, India narrowed the production gap with China to just two months, up from six to nine months previously. The iPhone 15 was the first model Apple manufactured in India to be ready for the global launch from day one.
Suppliers, including Foxconn, have also shifted from importing complete circuit boards to assembling components directly in India. Motherboard manufacturing alone is expected to improve the trade balance by $2.1 billion in the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
However, the outlook remains uncertain. Strong demand for memory chips from data centers is driving up the price of semiconductors used in phones. Meanwhile, demand for phones in the Indian market is declining, especially in the low-cost segment. This could reduce component imports, but weaker global smartphone sales also risk impacting exports.
Subsidies are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Five years ago, India implemented a subsidy program equivalent to 4-6% of the finished phone bill value to offset infrastructure disadvantages and production costs. As chip prices rise due to demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) sector, the budget may have to bear additional support costs.
With a subsidy rate of 4%, for every additional $1 billion in the bill value solely due to rising chip prices, the budget would have to spend an extra $40 million. Thus, even if production doesn't increase proportionally, the cost of subsidies could still balloon.
To move further into the supply chain, the Indian government has allocated an additional $13.4 billion to develop the domestic semiconductor industry. However, the $10 billion subsidy introduced five years ago has mainly helped establish overseas chip packaging facilities, failing to create advanced chip manufacturing capabilities.
Advanced chip manufacturing requires cutting-edge technology, significant capital investment, and the ability to accept long periods without profitability. India still faces challenges in all three areas. Even Tata Group, a key Apple partner in the country and the company behind India's only semiconductor manufacturing plant project, is facing disputes over control and concerns related to the scale of investment in the electronics sector.
International experience shows that moving up to higher-tech stages is not easy. Malaysia developed chip packaging and circuit board assembly operations from the 1970s, but its progress up the value chain stalled after the country reached upper-middle income status in 1992. Meanwhile, South Korea and Taiwan (China) leveraged the semiconductor industry to rise to the ranks of wealthy economies.
It's not easy to copy the Chinese model.
India can hardly rely solely on billions of dollars in investment to quickly catch up with the world's leading high-tech manufacturing hubs. Instead, it needs to develop its design and engineering capabilities while allocating resources to healthcare, education, climate change response, and labor-intensive industries such as textiles, footwear, and toys.

The Chinese model is particularly difficult to replicate. Apple's success in the country is linked to Foxconn's ability to coordinate with local authorities to rapidly build large-scale factory complexes. This combination of deployment speed, production scale, and risk tolerance is an advantage that India will find difficult to replicate.
Apple may be able to help India improve its manufacturing capabilities and become more deeply involved in the global supply chain, but that doesn't mean the country will become the next factory of the world. Continuing to increase subsidies in the hope of replicating the Chinese model could lead to ever-increasing costs without necessarily delivering commensurate benefits.
From attracting investment to mastering technology: Lessons for Vietnam
Drawing lessons from India's experience, Vietnam can develop high-tech industries in line with the spirit of Resolution 57-NQ/TW dated December 22, 2024, of the Politburo on breakthroughs in national science, technology, innovation, and digital transformation. Investment incentives may attract large corporations, but they cannot replace endogenous technological capabilities and the ability to master high value-added processes.
Therefore, support policies need to be linked to tangible results such as technology transfer, development of supporting industries, training of high-quality human resources, and enhancement of research, design, and manufacturing capabilities. Regular evaluation of budget utilization efficiency is also essential to limit prolonged reliance on incentives without building sustainable competitiveness.
More importantly, Vietnam needs to focus on investing in research and development, digital infrastructure, education, and linkages between businesses and research institutions. This is the foundation for science, technology, and innovation to truly become a driving force for productivity enhancement, helping domestic businesses move up to higher value-added stages in the global supply chain, instead of primarily relying on processing and assembly.
