How close is the India-US trade deal to becoming reality? After months of negotiations, tariff disputes and uncertainty over Russian oil purchases, officials on both sides are signalling progress. But External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has offered a reminder that optimism is not the same as a signed agreement.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit in New Delhi on Thursday, Jaishankar said the negotiations were moving towards completion, while cautioning that the final stretch could still throw up challenges. "Well, look, it's never done till it's done."
His remarks come after US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also expressed confidence that the long-pending pact could be concluded soon.
How close is the India-US trade deal to being signed?
Jaishankar said negotiators were working through the remaining hurdles but declined to reveal the details. "What you've heard not just from Secretary Rubio, but from Minister Piyush Goyal, from others, from me, is that we are moving towards it. But, as I said, often the last mile or the penultimate miles do pose their challenges. I think the [negotiating] teams are working through them now."
He added: "If you're asking me to tell you what exactly those challenges are, I'm sorry I won't. That's for the negotiators to sort out."
The latest comments follow Rubio’s October 20 meeting with Jaishankar in Mumbai. Speaking to reporters, Rubio said the countries were close to an agreement, with only a small number of issues left to resolve. In an interview with The Indian Express, he said the deal could be weeks, rather than months, away, while stressing that the wording must be agreed upon by both sides.
Trump, meanwhile, said on October 20 that the countries were “pretty close” and suggested the agreement would be “a much different kind of deal” from previous US trade pacts, without explaining what that would mean in practice.
Why has the India-US trade agreement taken so long?
India and the US began pursuing a bilateral trade agreement in February 2025. Negotiations have been complicated by disagreements over tariffs, market access, agricultural products and industrial goods, alongside wider tensions over India’s purchases of Russian oil.
The two countries announced a framework for the first phase of the agreement in February 2026, but changes in US tariff policy prompted further discussions. As The Indian Express reported, negotiators have since been working to bridge differences over the terms and the tariff treatment of Indian exports.
What do Russian oil and energy have to do with the deal?
Energy has become an important part of the wider diplomatic conversation. During his India visit, Rubio said greater energy trade with the US could help India diversify its supply chains. He also described India as a refining “superpower” and discussed the possibility of Indian refineries processing more Venezuelan crude.
Rubio said India had made progress in diversifying its energy sources. His remarks followed Washington’s recent pause on certain proposed tariffs linked to purchases of Russian energy, easing one complication in the negotiations.
What happens next for the India-US trade deal?
The Ministry of External Affairs said Jaishankar and Rubio reviewed cooperation across trade, defence, technology and energy security, reaffirming their commitment to the wider strategic partnership.
For now, the key question is whether the remaining differences can be resolved and translated into an agreed text. The latest statements suggest momentum, but no final trade deal has been announced.
Jaishankar’s caution remains the most important caveat: until both sides settle the terms and formally complete the agreement, the finish line is not yet crossed.

SMEStreet Exclusive Analysis | As Washington and New Delhi move closer to concluding their long-awaited bilateral trade agreement, Rubio’s engagements in Mumbai and Jamnagar bring trade, energy security, technology, geopolitics and the future of Indian exporters into sharper focus.
By Dr Faiz Askari, Founder & Chief Editor, SMEStreet
New Delhi, October 21, 2026: When US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India, the significance of his visit extended far beyond conventional diplomacy. At a time when international trade is increasingly influenced by tariffs, energy disruptions, geopolitical rivalries and changing supply chains, his engagements in Mumbai and Jamnagar have placed India–US economic cooperation at an important crossroads.
For India, the visit presents an opportunity to restore momentum to a strategically important relationship that has experienced its share of economic disagreements. For Washington, it is an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with a major economic and geopolitical partner while expanding American commercial interests in energy, defence and technology.
For Indian industry, however, the most important question is straightforward: Will the diplomatic optimism translate into commercially meaningful advantages for Indian exporters, manufacturers, service providers and MSMEs?
Rubio has indicated that negotiations on the India–US Bilateral Trade Agreement are approaching completion, with only a limited number of issues remaining unresolved. In an interview with The Indian Express, he suggested that approximately 99% of the work had been completed and that finalisation could be a matter of weeks rather than months.
Although this offers considerable encouragement, an important distinction remains. A trade agreement approaching completion is not the same as an agreement being signed, ratified and implemented.
It is precisely this difference that Indian industry will be watching.
Rubio–Jaishankar Meeting: Trade Negotiations Enter a Critical Phase
On October 20, Rubio met External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar in Mumbai, where discussions covered trade, energy security, defence, emerging technologies and wider international developments.
Both governments reaffirmed the importance of strengthening the India–US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership and welcomed progress in negotiations on the Bilateral Trade Agreement.
The discussions also touched upon energy security and developments in the Middle East, demonstrating the extent to which geopolitical challenges have become inseparable from the economic relationship.
The visit represents an important effort to rebuild confidence at a time when differences over American tariffs, India's purchases of Russian oil and several trade-related concerns have created uncertainty.
The underlying strategic interests, however, remain substantial.
India offers the United States a rapidly expanding consumer market, a significant manufacturing base, a large technology workforce and an important role in Indo-Pacific security.
The United States, meanwhile, remains a major destination for Indian exports, a source of technology and investment, and a strategically important partner for India's industrial and economic development.
The bilateral relationship is therefore too commercially significant to remain hostage to recurring disagreements.
How Close Is the India–US Trade Deal?
One of the strongest messages emerging from Rubio's visit is that both sides believe a negotiated breakthrough is within reach.
The February 2026 trade framework had already provided a basis for reducing some tariff-related tensions. Under that arrangement, Washington announced a reduction in its reciprocal tariff on India to 18%, alongside the removal of an additional 25% tariff associated with Russian oil purchases. Product-specific duties and other trade measures require separate consideration.
The negotiations since then have focused on converting the broader understanding into enforceable commitments.
On October 15, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal indicated that the first tranche of the agreement was undergoing final legal drafting.
He also made an economically important point: India intends to proceed when the agreement provides its exporters with a competitive or comparable advantage against rival exporting economies.
This is particularly relevant because India does not compete in the American market in isolation.
Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and several other economies compete directly with India in products ranging from garments and footwear to consumer goods and manufactured components.
If Indian exporters obtain less favourable market-access conditions than their competitors, the commercial value of an agreement could be significantly reduced.
Consequently, India is seeking more than tariff reductions. It is seeking a predictable and competitively fair trading environment.
What can realistically be expected from the agreement?
The immediate priority is likely to be the conclusion of the pending first tranche, including clarity on tariff commitments, preferential market access and the legal language governing implementation.
Further progress could emerge in technology trade, energy purchases, customs facilitation, rules of origin, standards recognition and investment cooperation.
Nevertheless, expectations should remain measured. The precise benefits for any industry will depend on the final tariff schedules, exemptions, product coverage and implementation provisions.
The timing of an announcement is also not guaranteed. Rubio's optimism strengthens the expectation of an early conclusion, but the agreement must still satisfy the commercial and political requirements of both countries.
Why This Visit Is Economically More Important Than It Appears
According to figures published by the Embassy of India in Washington, bilateral goods and services trade between India and the United States reached approximately $241.66 billion during calendar year 2025.
India's merchandise exports to the American market accounted for approximately $103.82 billion, while bilateral services trade exceeded $92 billion.
These figures establish the scale of the relationship.
A change in tariff treatment, customs procedures or market-access rules can influence billions of dollars in commercial transactions.
For Indian businesses, these decisions affect actual order books, pricing negotiations, manufacturing schedules, working capital requirements and employment.
For American businesses, India offers opportunities in energy, advanced manufacturing, civil aviation, digital infrastructure, healthcare technologies and defence-related supply chains.
However, the trade relationship is not without competing interests.
Washington is seeking greater access for American goods and technology, while India must ensure that market-opening commitments do not disproportionately affect vulnerable domestic industries.
A successful agreement will therefore have to balance two objectives: strengthening bilateral trade and protecting the competitiveness of strategically important sectors.
Jamnagar and the Energy Question: Why Oil Diplomacy Matters
Rubio's engagement with Reliance Industries and his visit to the company's Jamnagar refining complex demonstrate how energy security has moved to the centre of contemporary diplomacy.
The United States has expressed interest in encouraging increased processing of Venezuelan crude through Indian refining facilities, with potential discussions extending to upstream opportunities.
Reliance's substantial refining infrastructure makes Jamnagar strategically relevant to international petroleum trade, particularly during periods of supply disruption.
For India, the commercial implications extend beyond a single corporate group.
Access to diversified crude supplies can support energy resilience, while stable petroleum availability is important for domestic manufacturing and logistics.
Yet diversification is not automatically equivalent to lower energy costs. Shipping expenses, crude quality, refining economics, geopolitical restrictions and global oil prices will continue to determine the actual advantage.
For Indian MSMEs, energy diplomacy may appear removed from everyday business operations. Its consequences, however, are immediate.
Higher fuel prices increase transportation costs. Expensive petroleum derivatives raise input costs for plastics, chemicals, packaging and several manufacturing sectors. Volatile energy markets complicate pricing and inventory decisions.
Greater supply reliability would therefore be beneficial to the wider industrial ecosystem, provided it translates into improved domestic price stability.
Rubio's Jamnagar engagement also demonstrates India's increasing importance as an industrial and energy-processing partner rather than merely a large consumer of imported petroleum.
The Russian Oil Issue: Can Trade and Strategic Autonomy Coexist?
One of the most complicated aspects of India–US relations has been India's continued purchase of Russian crude oil.
Washington has sought to use economic pressure in response to the Russia–Ukraine conflict. India, however, has consistently had to consider its own energy requirements, import dependence and economic interests.
The recent American waiver of additional sanctions-related tariffs has improved the immediate environment for trade negotiations.
Rubio has acknowledged the difficulty of balancing sanctions policy with the economic consequences for partner nations.
This development may indicate a more pragmatic approach, but it does not mean that every disagreement over Russian oil has disappeared.
For New Delhi, the long-term challenge is to preserve strategic autonomy while maintaining constructive relationships with the United States, Russia, Europe and other major partners.
For Washington, the challenge is to deepen cooperation with India without demanding alignment on every foreign-policy issue.

The US president did not offer any details on how the deal would be different, or when it is likely to be finalized
US President Donald Trump has said he expects the finalization of a "much different kind" of trade deal with India soon, boosting hopes that a breakthrough is near after months-long negotiations appear to have stalled over bilateral trade concessions.
Earlier this month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the negotiations hit a "plateau," making further concessions difficult for both sides.
India, which currently faces 10% tariffs on exports to the US, has sought an advantage over its competitors in South Asia in the American market. In return, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government is willing to allow market access to US companies, apart from some sectors in which local industries could be harmed.
"They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah... It's going to be a much different kind of a deal than we've done," Trump told reporters at the Oval Office on Tuesday.
The US president did not explain what he meant by a "much different deal" and did not provide a time frame.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday in Mumbai that a deal could be reached in weeks, adding that the countries are "as close as you can be without having an executed agreement." Rubio is in India to tap the country's "refining superpower" status to cool global oil prices.
A trade deal would offer a significant boost to a host of India's export-oriented sectors, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, electronics, and information technology-related services, NDTV reported.
The recent passage of the Russia sanctions act - which gave Trump the authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on Russia's top oil buyers, including India - frayed ties and threatened to stall the trade talks.
Trump, however, suspended these sanctions last week, in what was seen as a conciliatory gesture to New Delhi.

The report highlighted the importance of maintaining a certain difference between Indian and G7 interest rates to attract foreign debt capital, particularly as the US Federal Reserve is expected to continue its rate-hiking cycle.
External member of the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), Saugata Bhattacharya, said that "maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows".
The report said this consideration has become relevant alongside concerns about the domestic inflation outlook and the possibility of further increases in input costs being passed on to consumers.
The minutes of the RBI's October MPC meeting highlighted growing inflation risks, with the central bank's inflation projection for the third quarter of FY27 reaching 6 per cent, the upper limit of its 2-6 per cent tolerance band.
Despite these inflation concerns, India's economic growth has remained resilient. The country recorded GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of FY27, supported by strong private consumption, a pickup in exports and continued momentum in the services sector.
The report noted that some MPC members believe the RBI needs to respond in a timely manner to prevent current price pressures from spreading further across the economy.
It also highlighted the risks posed by higher energy prices, supply-chain pressures and El Nino conditions to the growth outlook.
Based on the inflation outlook and global monetary policy developments, YES Bank expects the RBI to increase its policy repo rate by a cumulative 50 basis points, with a 25-basis-point hike in December and another 25-basis-point increase in February.
However, this remains the bank's forecast and not a decision announced by the RBI.
The report's assessment highlights the challenge facing monetary policymakers: addressing rising domestic inflation while also considering how India's interest rate differential with major developed economies may affect foreign debt capital flows.
